A second possibility is that it is to be taken at its apparent meaning: that they bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, acknowledging faith and denying hypocrisy from themselves. This is the more plausible view.(p-14)

The occasion of revelation of this verse is what Asbat narrated from al-Suddi: "Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul was with the Messenger of God ﷺ on a military expedition, and among them were Bedouin Arabs who followed the people. Ibn Ubayy used to prepare food for the Messenger of God ﷺ every day. A Bedouin drew water in a basin he had made of stones. A man from the companions of Ibn Ubayy came with a she-camel to water it from that water, but the Bedouin prevented him, and they fought, and the Bedouin wounded him in the head. The man came to Abdullah [ibn Ubayy] with his blood running down his face, and it grieved him. Abdullah then acted hypocritically and said: 'What is wrong with them? May God send their affair to ruin.' He said to his companions: 'Do not bring Muhammad any food until the Bedouins disperse from him.' Zayd ibn Arqam heard this, and he was a youth, so he informed his paternal uncle, and his uncle came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and related it to him. He sent for Ibn Ubayy, who was one of the most handsome of people and the most eloquent in speech. He came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and swore: 'By He who sent you with the truth, I did not say any of this.' He (the Prophet) believed him, and God revealed this verse." ﴿And God knows that you are truly His Messenger.﴾ That is: even if those who are hypocritical towards you are hypocritical, God knows that you are His Messenger, so they will not harm you.

Then He said: ﴿And God bears witness that the hypocrites are surely liars.﴾ This has two possible meanings:

One: God swears that the hypocrites are surely liars in their oaths.

Two: its meaning is that God knows that the hypocrites are surely liars in it.

﴿They have taken their oaths as a shield (junnah).﴾ The junnah is the covering that protects from harm, and from this is the saying of al-A'sha Maymun:

"If you do not make a shield for your honour from wealth, blame will travel every road."

In this there are two views:

One: from captivity and killing, so that they may protect by them their blood and their property. This is the view of Qatadah.

Two: from death, so that they will not have the funeral prayer offered over them, and thus their hypocrisy would become evident to all the Muslims. This is the meaning of al-Suddi's view.

It may also be understood, thirdly, as a shield that averts from them the disgrace of hypocrisy.(p-15)

﴿So they barred (others) from the way of God.﴾ In this there are two views:

One: from Islam, by repelling the Muslims from it.

Two: from jihad, by discouraging the Muslims, spreading rumours about it, and separating themselves from them. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said: "I do not fear for you two kinds of men: a believer whose faith is established, and a disbeliever whose disbelief is established. But I fear for you a hypocrite who seeks refuge in faith while acting otherwise."

﴿And when you see them, their bodies please you.﴾ That is, the goodliness of their appearance and the completeness of their form.

﴿And if they speak, you listen to what they say.﴾ That is, because of the sweetness of their speech and the eloquence of their words.

A second possibility is: because of the display of Islam and their mention of agreement.

﴿As if they were propped-up pieces of wood.﴾ In this there are three sayings:

One: He likened them to upright palm trees because of the goodliness of their appearance.

Two: [He likened them] to rotten pieces of wood because of the badness of their inner state.

Three: He likened them to propped-up pieces of wood because they do not hear guidance nor accept it, just as propped-up wood does not hear it. This was said by al-Kalbi. His saying ﴿propped up﴾ is because they lean upon faith to secure their blood.

﴿They think every cry is against them.﴾ In this there are three aspects:

One: because of their fear and their wickedness, they think every cry they hear, even if a man calls to his companion or shouts to his she-camel, is that the enemy has overwhelmed them and that death has descended upon them. This was said by al-Suddi.

Two: ﴿They think every cry is against them﴾ is a statement whose pronoun does not require what follows it. One: its meaning is "may God curse them." This was said by Ibn Abbas and Abu Malik.

One: its meaning is "how are they lying." This was said by Ibn Abbas.

Two: its meaning is "how are they turning away from the truth." This was said by Qatadah.

Three: its meaning is "how are they being turned away from right guidance." This was said by al-Hasan.

Four: its meaning is "how have their minds gone astray from this." This was said by al-Suddi.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 63, verses 5–8:

﴿When it is said to them, "Come, the Messenger of God will ask forgiveness for you,"﴾ and so on.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ), whenever he halted at a place, would not depart from it until he had prayed there. When the expedition of Tabuk took place, news reached him that Ibn Ubayy had said: "If we return to Medina, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it." So he set out before the last of the people had halted. It was said to Abdullah ibn Ubayy: "Go to the Prophet (ﷺ) so that he may ask forgiveness for you," but he turned his head away. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿they turned their heads﴾, referring to him and his companions, that is, they shook them and turned away to the right and to the left, away from the direction of the one addressing them, looking sideways.

It is possible to take a second meaning: the words ﴿the Messenger of God will ask forgiveness for you﴾ mean "he will ask you to repent of hypocrisy," because repentance is a form of seeking forgiveness.

Regarding what Abdullah ibn Ubayy did when he turned his head, there are two possibilities:

The first: he did it mockingly and in refusal to do what he was invited to, namely to come to the Messenger so that he would ask forgiveness for him. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: he turned his head meaning "what did you say?" This was said by Mujahid.

﴿And you see them turning away﴾: regarding this there are two meanings:

The first: they refrain. The poet said:

"You turned the cup away from us, Umm Amr, though the cup's course was to the right."

The second: they turn away. Al-A'sha said:

"Huraira has spoken truly about us, that she does not speak to us out of ignorance of Umm Khulayd, whoever you are bound to."

Regarding what they turn away from, there are two meanings:

The first: from what they were invited to, namely the Messenger of God (ﷺ) asking forgiveness for them.

The second: from sincerity in faith.

﴿while they are arrogant﴾: regarding this there are two meanings:

The first: they are proud.

The second: they are refusing.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 63, verses 9–11:

﴿O you who have believed, let not your wealth or your children divert you from the remembrance of Allah﴾. In it there are four interpretations:

First: that by "the remembrance of Allah" is meant the obligatory prayer (al-salah al-maktubah). This was said by ʿAtaʾ.

Second: that it means the obligations of Allah which He has enjoined, including prayer and other than it. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Third: that it means obedience to Allah in jihad. This was said by al-Kalbi.

Fourth: that it means fear of Allah at the time of His remembrance.

﴿And spend from what We have provided you﴾. In it there are two interpretations:

One: that it refers to the obligatory zakat from wealth. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Second: that it refers to voluntary charity, supporting the needy, and aiding the one in distress.

﴿And Allah will never delay a soul when its term has come﴾. It admits two interpretations:

One: that He will never delay it from death once its term has expired, and this is the more apparent of the two.

Second: that He will never delay it after death; rather, He only hastens for it [the reckoning] in the grave.
